framework.model: A journey is a JSON object: id, title, source chapter + section, an ordered node list (id, label, chapterText, explanation, alsoIn cross-references) and an edge list. The renderer draws the same nodes twice: once as an accessible ordered list (the authoritative content, usable with no JavaScript) and once as a static SVG diagram (visual overview, with the list as its text alternative). Future journeys add one JSON file and one route section; no new diagram code is needed.
rules: Every node carries a source chapter reference.
No node may be added without chapter text behind it.
No 3D, no GPU-heavy rendering, no large dependencies; the diagram is inline SVG.
The interactive stepper is progressive enhancement loaded with defer; all content is present without it.

chapter.title: From silicon to a working NIC

nodes.chapterText: The OS identifies a PCIe function and its identifiers.
nodes.explanation: The operating system finds the network card on the PCIe bus and identifies what it is. Without this step there is nothing for a driver to bind to.
nodes.label: PCIe device discovery

nodes.chapterText: A compatible kernel driver initializes the device.
nodes.explanation: A compatible kernel driver takes control of the hardware. The chapter's data-path summary puts it plainly: the device driver controls the hardware and its queues.
nodes.label: Driver binding

nodes.chapterText: The driver exposes a network interface and packet queues.
nodes.explanation: The driver exposes a network interface and packet queues to the kernel. From here the Linux network stack processes IP and transport, and applications use socket interfaces.
nodes.label: Kernel interface

alsoIn.note: Routes determine forwarding next hops; ip route manipulates kernel routing tables.

nodes.explanation: Network configuration gives the interface its addresses and routes, so IP-layer reachability exists. The chapter's worked example adds that the kernel selects routes and interfaces and handles IP and transport processing.
nodes.label: Addressing and routes

alsoIn.note: The fuller port-to-service journey: NIC receives frame, DMA to memory, interrupt or polling, kernel driver, Ethernet/IP processing, routing, socket, user-space server.

nodes.chapterText: Sockets, kernel protocols and NIC exchange packets.
nodes.explanation: Packets actually move: the chapter's example is a web server receiving an Ethernet frame, processing TCP/IP in the kernel, then passing payload bytes to an application socket. In the outbound direction the driver submits packet buffers and the NIC sends link-layer frames.
nodes.label: Packet transfer

journey.scopeNote: A teaching sequence from the chapter, not a literal execution path and not a historical timeline. The chapter itself states the real network stack is bidirectional and contains additional details such as ARP/neighbor discovery, MTU, offloads and retransmissions.
journey.title: NIC packet path

workedExample.caveat: The network card does not directly understand an HTTPS URL. The operating system and applications perform different jobs.
steps: Browser resolves a hostname and prepares a request (DNS returns an IP address).
TCP establishes a connection and TLS protects application traffic (HTTP/3 instead uses QUIC over UDP).
The kernel selects routes and interfaces and handles IP and transport processing.
The driver configures NIC transmit descriptors and device queues and submits a packet buffer.
The NIC sends link-layer frames through its physical or virtual interface; Ethernet frames travel to a local switch.
Switches and routers forward traffic toward its destination; the remote server responds.
